source_text: Quaestionem rursus de curatione sabbatis facta quomodo discussit? unusquisque uestrum sabbatis non soluits asinum aut bouem suum a praesepi et ducit ad potum? ergo secundum condicionem legis operatus legem confirmauit, non dissoluit, iubentem nullum opus fieri, nisi quod fieret omni animae, quanto potius humanae? Parabolarum congruentiam ubique recognoscor exigere. simile est regnum dei, inquit, grano sinapis, quod accepit homo et seminauit in horto suo. quis in persona hominis intellegendus? utique Christus, qui, licet Marcionis, filius hominis est dictus, qui accepit a patre semen regni, sermonem scilicet euangelii, et seminauit in horto, isto utique in mundo. puta nunc in homine, sed cum in (suo) horto dixerit nec mundus autem nec homo illius sit, sed creatoris, ergo qui in suum seminarit creatoris ostenditur. aut si, ut hunc laqueum euadant, conuerterint hominis personam a Christo in hominem accipientem semen regni et seminantem in horto cordis sui, nec ipsa materia alii conueniet quam creatori. De sequenti plane similitudine uereor, ne forte alterius dei regnum portendat. fermento enim comparauit illud, non azymis, quae familiariora sunt creatori. congruit et haec coniectura mendicantibus argumenta. itaque et ego uanitatem uanitate depellam, fermentationem quoque congruere dicens regno creatoris, quia post illam clibanus uel furnus gehennae sequatur. quale est enim, ut (sit) lenissimi dei regnum quod etiam iudicii feruor lacrimosa austeritate subsequitur? Quotiens adhuc se iudicem ostendit et in iudice creatorem! quotiens utique reicit et damnat reiciendo! sicut hic quoque: cum surrexerit, inquit, pater familiae — quo? nisi quo dixit Esaias: cum surrexerit comminuere terram - et cluserit ostium — utique excludendis iniquis, quibus pulsantibus respondebit: nescio unde sitis, et rursus, enumerantibus quod coram illo ederint et biberint et in plateis eorum docuerit [adiciet]: recedite a me omnes, operarii iniquitatis —, illic erit fletus et dentium frendor, — ubi? foris scilicet, ubi erunt exclusi ostio cluso; ab eo ergo erit poena, a quo fit exclusio in poenam — \'cum uidebunt iustos introeuntes in regnum dei, se uero detineri foris\'. a quo? si a creatore, quis ergo erit intus recipiens iustos in regnum? deus bonus? quid ergo illic creatori? ut foris detineat in poenam quos aduersarius eius exclusit? suscipiendos a se, si utique, magis in aduersarii bilem. sed et ille, exclusurus iniquos, sciat utique creatorem illos detenturum in poenam aut non sciat oportet. ergo aut nolente eo detinebuntur, et minor est illo, qui detinet, cedens ei nolens, aut si uult ita fieri, ipse ita faciendum iudicauit. et non erit melior creatore ipse auctor infamiae creatoris. haec si nulla ratione consistunt, ut alius punire alius liberare credatur, unius erit tam iudicium quam et regnum, et dum unius est utrumque, qui et iudicat, creatoris est.
pass_a_gloss: The question about the healing on the Sabbath, how did He discuss it? Does not each one of you on the Sabbath untie his donkey or ox from the manger and lead it to water? Therefore, according to the condition of the law, He operated the law, He confirmed it, not dissolved it, commanding that no work be done, except what would be done for every soul, how much more for a human one? I recognize that the congruence of parables is required everywhere. The kingdom of God, He says, is similar to a grain of mustard, which a man took and sowed in his garden. Who is to be understood in the person of the man? Certainly Christ, who, even if according to Marcion, is called the Son of man, who received from the Father the seed of the kingdom, namely the sermon of the gospel, and sowed it in the garden, certainly in this world. Suppose now in the man, but since He said in his garden, and neither the world nor the man is His, but the Creator's, therefore He who sows in His own is shown to be the Creator's. Or if, in order to avoid this snare, they turn the person of the man from Christ to a man receiving the seed of the kingdom and sowing it in the garden of his heart, not even this matter will be suitable for anyone other than the Creator. I fear the next plain similitude, lest it perhaps portend the kingdom of another god. For He compared it to leaven, not to unleavened bread, which is more familiar to the Creator. This conjecture also suits those who are begging for arguments. And so I also will repel vanity with vanity, saying that fermentation is also suitable for the kingdom of the Creator, because after it, the oven or furnace of Gehenna will follow. What kind of kingdom of a very mild god is it, which is also followed by the fervor of judgment with tearful austerity? How many times does He still show Himself as a judge and in the judge, the Creator! How many times does He reject and condemn by rejecting! Just as here also: when the father of the family rises, He says, and closes the door - certainly to exclude the wicked, to whom, when they knock, He will respond: I do not know where you are from, and again, when they enumerate what they ate and drank before Him and taught in their streets, He will add: depart from me, all you workers of iniquity - there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth - where? Certainly outside, where they will be excluded by the closed door; therefore, the punishment will be from Him, from whom the exclusion into punishment is made - 'when they see the just entering into the kingdom of God, but themselves being detained outside'. From whom? If from the Creator, who then will be inside, receiving the just into the kingdom? The good God? What then is the Creator doing there? So that outside, He detains in punishment those whom His adversary excluded? To be received by Him, if indeed, rather in the bitterness of the adversary. But also He, who is about to exclude the wicked, certainly knows that the Creator will detain them in punishment, or He ought not to know. Therefore, either they will be detained without His will, and He who detains is less than He, yielding to Him unwillingly, or if He wants it to be so, He Himself has judged that it should be done. And He will not be better than the Creator, being the author of the Creator's infamy. If these things do not consist of any reason, so that one is believed to punish and another to liberate, the judgment and the kingdom will be of one, and since both are of one, He who judges is the Creator's.

choices.why: to convey the sense of certainty

bible_refs.note: when the father of the family rises and closes the door

pass_b_english: How did he handle the question about healing on the Sabbath? "Doesn't each of you on the Sabbath untie his donkey or ox from the manger and lead it to water?" (Luke 13:15). So, acting in line with the law's own condition, he upheld the law; he did not dissolve it. The law commands that no work be done except what is done for the sake of any soul, how much more a human one? I see that the coherence of parables is required everywhere. "The kingdom of God is like a mustard seed, which a man took and sowed in his garden" (Luke 13:19). Who is meant by the man? Obviously Christ, who, even on Marcion's terms, is called the Son of Man. He received the seed of the kingdom from the Father — that is, the gospel message — and sowed it in his garden, which is this world. Suppose the 'man' is a human being; but since he said 'in his garden,' and neither the world nor the man belongs to the alien god but to the Creator, the one who sows in his own domain is shown to be the Creator's agent. Or if, to escape this trap, they shift the 'man' from Christ to a believer receiving the seed of the kingdom and sowing it in the garden of his heart, even that soil suits no one but the Creator.

I dread the next plain similitude, lest it betray the kingdom of another god. He compared it to leaven, not to unleavened bread, which is more familiar to the Creator. This conjecture suits those begging for arguments just fine. So I will drive out vanity with vanity and say fermentation fits the Creator's kingdom too, because after it comes the oven or furnace of Gehenna. What kind of kingdom belonging to a supremely mild god is followed by the fury of judgment with tearful severity? How often does he still show himself as a judge, and in the judge reveal the Creator? How often does he reject and condemn by rejecting? Just like here: "When the master of the house rises" — where? Nowhere but where Isaiah said: "When he rises to shake the earth" — "and shuts the door" (Luke 13:25), certainly to exclude the wicked. When they knock, he will answer, "I don't know where you're from," and again, when they list what they ate and drank in his presence and taught in their streets, he will add: "Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity" (Luke 13:27; Matthew 24:51). There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth — where? Outside, obviously, where they are excluded by the shut door. So the punishment comes from the one who executes the exclusion into punishment. "When they see the righteous entering the kingdom of God, but themselves thrown outside" (Luke 13:28). From whom? If from the Creator, who then is inside receiving the righteous into the kingdom? The 'good' god? What is the Creator doing there, then? Detaining in punishment outside those whom his adversary excluded? They would be received by him, if anything, rather in the adversary's spite. But the one who is about to exclude the wicked must surely know that the Creator will detain them in punishment — or he ought not to know. Therefore either they are detained against his will, and the one who detains is inferior to him, yielding to him unwillingly, or if he wants it that way, he himself has judged it so. And he will be no better than the Creator, since he becomes the author of the Creator's infamy. If these things hold together by no logic at all, so that one is supposed to punish and another to liberate, then both the judgment and the kingdom belong to one God. And since both belong to one, the one who judges is the Creator's.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological arguments regarding the identity of the Creator and the continuity of the Law. Scripture citations in Pass B (Luke 13:15, 13:19, 13:25, 13:27, 13:28, Matthew 24:51, and Isaiah) are correctly identified and added to the text to clarify the parables and prophecies being discussed, matching the Latin content (e.g., 'cum surrexerit comminuere terram' matched to Isaiah). Pass A and B are consistent with the Latin source.
